items.q: In Mitchell's definition, a learning task is well-defined by the triple:
items.explain: Performance measure P, Task T, and Experience E. Performance at T (measured by P) improves with E.

items.q: An automated (self-driving) vehicle that learns from recorded human-driver images and steering commands is primarily an example of:
items.explain: It learns a mapping from labelled input (images) to outputs (steering) — supervised learning. (A classic slide-marked answer.)

items.q: Which paradigm is also called 'exploratory learning'?
items.explain: Unsupervised learning explores unlabelled data for hidden structure — no target variable to aim at.

items.q: Customer segmentation and market segmentation are applications of:
items.explain: Grouping customers by similarity with no labels is clustering.

items.q: A generative model learns which distribution?
items.explain: Generative models learn the joint $p(x,y)$ and can generate samples; discriminative models learn $p(y\mid x)$.

items.q: For 4 binary features, the number of distinct instances and the number of possible concepts are:
items.explain: Instances $=2^4=16$; concepts $=2^{(2^4)}=2^{16}$ — every labelling of the 16 instances.

items.q: Two attributes with 2 values each. How many semantically distinct conjunctive hypotheses (including '?' and reject-all)?
items.explain: $(2+1)(2+1)+1 = 9+1 = 10$. The +1 collapses all reject-all (∅) hypotheses into one.

items.q: The correct nesting of spaces is:
items.explain: Inductive bias shrinks Concept→Hypothesis; consistency with data shrinks Hypothesis→Version.

items.q: Find-S learns using:
items.explain: Find-S ignores negatives and generalises the most specific hypothesis over positive examples only.

items.q: Which is NOT a limitation of Find-S?
options: It cannot detect whether the data is inconsistent/noisy
It always finds the globally optimal decision tree
items.explain: Find-S has nothing to do with decision trees. Its real limitations: ignores negatives, no noise handling, no backtracking, outputs just one hypothesis.

items.q: A decision tree represents a target concept as a:
items.explain: Each root-to-leaf path is a conjunction; the tree ORs the paths together — a disjunction of conjunctions.

items.q: The entropy of a node containing 9 'yes' and 5 'no' (out of 14) is closest to:
items.explain: $-\tfrac{9}{14}\log_2\tfrac{9}{14}-\tfrac{5}{14}\log_2\tfrac{5}{14}\approx 0.94$.

items.q: The entropy of a perfectly pure node (all one class) is:
items.explain: With $p=1$, $-1\log_2 1 = 0$. No uncertainty.

items.q: ID3 selects the attribute that:
items.explain: Gain = entropy before − expected entropy after. ID3 greedily maximises it.

items.q: ID3's inductive bias is best described as:
options: A restriction bias from an incomplete hypothesis space
A preference bias for shorter trees (Occam's razor)
items.explain: ID3 searches the complete space of trees but PREFERS short trees with high-gain attributes near the root — a preference (search) bias.

items.q: A hypothesis h overfits if, compared to some h′, it has:
options: Higher train error and higher true error
Lower train error but higher true error
Lower train error and lower true error
Higher train error but lower true error
items.explain: Overfitting: better on training data but worse over the full distribution than an alternative h′.

items.q: In reduced-error pruning, a node is removed only if the pruned tree:
options: Performs no worse on the validation set
items.explain: Validation accuracy is the gate — prune while it does not decrease; stop when further pruning hurts.

items.q: When choosing a threshold for a continuous attribute, candidate thresholds are placed:
options: At midpoints where the class label changes
At the mean of the attribute
items.explain: Sort by the attribute, find adjacent pairs whose label differs, and test the midpoints — pick max gain.

items.q: A model with low training error but high test error most likely has:
items.explain: A large train→test gap signals high variance (overfitting).

items.q: Total expected error decomposes as:
items.explain: $\text{Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \sigma^2$. The $\sigma^2$ term is irreducible.

items.q: A logistic-regression output $h_\theta(x)=0.2$ implies (select all that apply):
items.explain: $h_\theta(x)=P(y=1\mid x)=0.2$, so $P(y=0\mid x)=0.8$.

items.q: Squared-error cost is avoided in logistic regression because it becomes:
items.explain: With the sigmoid inside, squared error is non-convex; the log-loss restores convexity.

items.q: Which pairing is correct?
items.explain: Decision trees build a global model (eager); KNN defers all work to query time (lazy).

items.q: For KNN regression, the prediction for a query is the ___ of its k neighbours; for classification it is the ___.
items.explain: Regression → mean of neighbours' values; classification → mode (majority class).

items.q: Setting k very large in KNN tends to cause:
items.explain: Large k averages over many points → predicts the majority class → high bias (underfitting).

items.q: Why must features be normalised before KNN?
options: So large-range attributes don't dominate the distance
To reduce the number of neighbours
items.explain: Distance is scale-sensitive; an attribute like income (large magnitude) would swamp age unless standardised.

items.q: On a 99% / 1% imbalanced fraud dataset, a classifier predicting 'not fraud' for everything achieves high accuracy but is useless. The better metric is:
items.explain: Recall captures how many actual frauds are caught; accuracy is misleading under class imbalance.

items.q: Precision is defined as:
items.explain: Precision = TP / (TP+FP): of those predicted positive, how many truly are. (TP/(TP+FN) is recall.)

items.q: The F1 score is the:
options: Arithmetic mean of precision and recall
Harmonic mean of precision and recall
items.explain: $F1 = 2PR/(P+R)$ — the harmonic mean, which punishes a low value in either.

items.q: An ROC AUC of 0.5 means the classifier:
items.explain: AUC 0.5 sits on the diagonal — no discriminative power. AUC 1 is perfect, 0 is perfectly inverted.
